utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Tell us what were the military investigative prisons that you knew about during the time you were commanding the HVO Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, sir. All I know -- well, what's military investigative, what's central, what the military prosecutor's job is, I don't know. I'm not informed about that to the extent to which I could give you any correct or relevant assessment. I knew that Heliodrom existed. I knew about Dretelj, and I sent people, according to the documents that you -- that's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, let's -- let's talk about the Heliodrom for a moment. Did you ever go there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Never?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. Well, never during the war. Afterwards there was some sort of celebration, two, three years after the war. That's when I went to Heliodrom -- or, rather, Heliodrom is a large -- well, there was an HVO brigade put up there, and I think there was a joint army there of the federation or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you never went to the Heliodrom. Did you ever see prisoners at the Heliodrom during 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And just to be super clear, when I say prisoners, that includes detainees, people in isolation, Muslims, Croats, Serbs. You never saw anyone who was in detention at the Heliodrom during 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the fifth time: In 1993 I never set foot in Heliodrom. I didn't see anybody. I had no reasonable grounds to do so or time or information, for heaven's sake.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What about in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992? 1992. Well, in 1992 I was not at Heliodrom. In 1992, I was -- that is to say in June when we liberated that there, then part of the unit moved forward as I was up at the line. In 1992, in June, I was there. After that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in June of 1992, you were there. Did you see prisoners there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. On those premises you had the Yugoslav People's Army and the Army of Republika Srpska. They were on the surrounding hills, and in that action of liberation, it seems to me -- well, if I toured the area, I probably toured that area but not Heliodrom, the Neretva River and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well -- now, General, are you telling us that you never knew during 1993 that any of these Muslim men who were being arrested or isolated were being held at the Heliodrom facility?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dear sir, I've already told you once that in September, the 4th or 5th of September in actual fact, I gave permission to a journalist from the magazine Globus, and on the basis of which permit and permission he wasn't able to enter, because he was told - and you'll have his statement - that as far as permission from Praljak was concerned, it wasn't worth a penny and that Tole gave him position [as interpreted] later on. As the guard changed, then they allowed this journalist to enter. But five or six days later, I happened to see in that particular magazine that there were prisoners, but, Mr. Stringer, that was not an area of responsibility of the commander of the Main Staff that I was, nor was the information that I read, nor did it indicate anything. Everything I learnt, I learnt subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, General --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: So let me repeat for the umpteenth time --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay, you've set out your position. Then what you're telling us is, and you'll correct me if I'm wrong, you learned about prisoners at the Heliodrom sometime by mid-September after the article was published, but you never went to the Heliodrom to look at the prisoners or the conditions because you didn't think it was part of your responsibility. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not. It's not. First of all, the journalist didn't enter Heliodrom. It was Gabela or Dretelj. I can't remember now which. Secondly, you keep wanting to add some time to the person who was sitting there. I had no information. I had no time in which to receive information of any kind, sir, because during that time I was releasing Muslim prisoners, letting a helicopter fly to save a Muslim doctor and a Muslim child. I was fighting at the front. So leave your constructions at home. I said no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, General, you just told us that the journalist came to you and that after -- and that after that, five or six days later, you happened to see in that particular magazine that there were prisoners. So what you're telling us, General, is that you didn't know about any prisoners based upon information available to you as commander of the HVO Main Staff, but you did have the means to learn about prisoners from reading about it in the media. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read about it not in the media but in one medium, that is to say in a magazine where that journalist had an article, and the magazine's name was Globus. So you, sir, or Judges, sentencing people, you don't ask who the people are in prison. You can't go to a prison and ask how they are, how they're doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want to make out it was a Stalinistic totalitarianism, or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You're claim that as commander of the HVO Main Staff you did not have the authority to go to Heliodrom, Gabela, Dretelj, Ljubuski in order to inspect the conditions there? That your assertion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you mean authority? How do you mean authority, did I have the authority? So in which little box of the commander of the Main Staff does he have the right and duty to do what you're talking about? What do you mean authority? I wasn't -- didn't have authority over prisons or of prisons in any shape or form. That's what I'm claiming.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I want to try to be a little bit more systematic about this. I think I know what your answer's going to be, maybe we can move through this quickly. During the time you were commander of the HVO Main Staff, did you ever learn that Muslim men were being held there at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If there were Muslim men being held at the Heliodrom, was the Main Staff, in your view, responsible for the conditions of their detention there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Gabela. When, and forgive me if I missed it, you just spoke about the September 5th, the journalist, the Globus article, the granting of access, does that relate to Dretelj or Gabela, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now. Either one or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Ljubuski. You've heard testimony, you've seen the documents, military investigative prison at Ljubuski. At any time during the period you were commanding the HVO Main Staff did you know about Muslim men being held prisoner at Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said you never went to Heliodrom. Did you ever go to Dretelj, Gabela, or Ljubuski during 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, you said that you were not responsible for any prisoners at the Heliodrom. General, tell us who or what body was responsible for the prisoners at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Was it the HVO Department of Defence and Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Was it Mr. Coric as head of the military police administration?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you have no knowledge as to who was responsible for the conditions and the treatment of prisoners being held at the Heliodrom during the time you're commander of the HVO Main Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And if I asked you the same question about Dretelj, Gabela, and Ljubuski, would your answer be the same?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to P04496. I'm going to skip ahead a little bit. 4496. General, this one is from the 25th of August, 1993. You are commander of the HVO Main Staff at this point in time. This is a report or a statement of reasons. It's issued to Brigadier Tole. It's coming from the deputy security commander of the 1st HVO Brigade, Knez Domagoj. Now, general, at this point in time Brigadier Tole, he's the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, but I think that the deputy commander for security, not of the brigade. The deputy security man in the brigade. That's what it says here, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. You're talking about the person who wrote this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And he's sending it to Brigadier Tole, who was the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brigadier Tole was the chief the Main Staff of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. So that -- and what -- the information that's being passed on to Brigadier Tole relates to the reasons why a particular person was released from prison, and then it describes the procedure and the priorities, et cetera. And it says: "The procedure, priorities, and the questions as to whether to release inmates from the prison has not been dealt with or defined by -- either by the operative zone South-east Herzegovina or the ministry. Because the lack of such instructions, we were forced to take our own decisions at the level of local HVO presidencies and brigade commands." And then it talks about the procedure for releasing inmates from Gabela and Dretelj. And here they could be released if they were married to a Croatian woman, if not of interest to security; or if they possessed letters of guarantee and a transit visa, if no interest to security; or if they are being sought by the Republic of Croatia with the necessary papers there. And then at the bottom it says: "The confusion surrounding releases from prison is due to ill-defined prisoner status, authority over prisoners, and the method of dealing with them, trials, exchanges," et cetera. "The subject of prisoners in this territory where they are the most numerous has been discussed on several occasions, and the leadership was informed of it both through the security service and through Commander Colonel Obradovic. Security service suggests that the matter of prisoners in this territory be dealt with urgently." Now, General, what this tells us, isn't it true, is that as of the 25th of August, 1993, we know that your Chief of Staff of your Main Staff has direct knowledge about prisoners being held at the Gabela and Dretelj prisons, these discriminatory criteria for release, if I can put it that way, releasing men who happened to be married to a Croatian woman. And so in fact information about the prisoners and the release criteria is information that's fully available to you as the commander of the Main Staff. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. From this it is clear that this was not sent to the Main Staff but to somebody personally, that is to say to Brigadier Tole personally. So then it's probable and logical that out of personal interest he sought information about what was happening. He was in the area, which is why -- I don't know why he asked that this be sent to him. It wasn't addressed to the Main Staff, to the commander of the Main Staff. Neither did Tole show me this, because it was a personal interest on his part in the matter. And here it says that the presidents of the HVO, that is to say of the municipalities, and that the leaders were informed, but not the leaders of the HVO about the problem in hand. So that's it. That's what this document is about. All you have to do is to read it carefully. There was probably some misunderstanding and Tole asked what this was all about. Not because it was his right to do but most probably because he had some reason to seek information and explanations as to what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, clearly Tole knew that there were prisoners down there at Dretelj and Gabela, and the fact is, General, that by late August of 1993 it was no secret. The media was on to it. Your Chief of Staff knew about it, and the sheer volume of prisoners involved makes it clear that someone in your position would have had full knowledge about the existence of these detention facilities. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me repeat for the 15th time when I learnt. On the 1st of September -- well, I'm saying this dozens of times, the existence of detainee centres does not change the situation. It is conduct that is important here. I sent people who had been sentenced to Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's go to P10924.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I have a follow-up question on this document. Looking at this document, it seems, and I say "it seems" because I don't want to draw any conclusions or make any statements, but it seems that Brigadier Tole obtained information on the conditions surrounding the release of Dr. Muhamed Durakovic. He was inquiring about these conditions and because of this the brigadier of the Knez Domagoj brigade is reporting to him and is telling him - you can see this in the document - that it's a complex matter; that it's difficult to know who does what. But as far as is Dr. Durakovic is concerned, he says that there was this question of transit visa, that the NUMA security service was also involved, and there was the president of HVO Mr. Bender, the commander of the new battalion, and the civilian police. All these people were involved. As a conclusion, it says that there is a lot of confusion around this. So any reasonable trier of fact looking at this document could draw this conclusion. Obviously at local level there's a lot of uncertainty on this issue, the issue of prisoners. You have an extensive knowledge of the politics prevailing at the time, so could you tell us whether -- how this Durakovic could be of interest to Tole in August. Either personally, that's your version of facts, or maybe for other reasons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't answer that question specifically. I think these can only be personal reasons. Obviously Tole addressed him personally. Information is forwarded to him in person, privately. It's not like -- it doesn't say "Chief of the Main Staff, Brigadier Tole." It says Brigadier Tole personally, here is the information you asked for. I don't know what the immediate cause was. I have no information on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will be very brief. We have a military document; this is obvious. And it is sent to Mr. Tole; there is no question about that. And this document deals with a detained person, but I note that in the first paragraph, given that there was a lack of instructions and the -- the local HVO presidencies and the brigade commands were consulted, and I will touch upon an issue that has already been mentioned here, namely the role of local political authorities. I do not know under which conditions Durakovic had been detained. Had there been an investigation, I don't know. All I can see is that political leaders of the HVO are being consulted, whereas in fact we are in the military arena. How do you explain this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Your Honour. I cannot provide any relevant information on this for your benefit regarding the confusion about this. My ignorance keeps me from furnishing you with any sort of answer at all for fear of getting it wrong. I don't know. The 25th of August I was probably on that convoy or some place. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may answer one thing, Your Honours. After the ZDF show, after the article that was published in Globus and then after Ed Vulliamy's piece, Mate Granic came over from Croatia, Silajdzic came, and they started dealing with this problem, and then I heard about this problem being dealt with. Franjo Tudjman went berserk, to put it that way. And then the whole thing started that September based on what the journalists had shown. But again this is not something that I was involved in or spending my time doing. I had heard about the exchanges that were under way, that the situation was being dealt with. In September in Bosnia-Herzegovina there were the attacks in Mostar by the BH Army, and they wanted to take everything, the hills and all of it. If you look at one thing first and then at the other separately, impression is that I had 24 hours to deal with each and every single thing. It's not in my job description, I don't have any information about this or about the text here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreter did not comprehend the last part of Mr. Praljak's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I've got to call you out on something you just said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We just learned from the interpreters that they did not understood the last part of your last sentence, so maybe you'll repeat it so that we have it in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did I say? I don't -- I no longer know what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The general doesn't really remember what he was saying, but we have the audiotape anyway. Go ahead, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, you just said after President Tudjman went berserk, et cetera, you said: "This is not something that I was involved in or spending my time doing. I heard about the exchanges that were under way, that the situation was being dealt with." General, you're the commander of the HVO Main Staff. I'm going to put to you it's not like an al a carte menu at a restaurant. You don't get to choose the things you're going to be responsible for, the things you're going to deal with. The fact is you know as of early September that there's a tremendous problem, an outcry based upon the conditions of these prisoners in these various HVO facilities. And in fact you were responsible and you could have done any number of things to look into the situation and to fix it. The fact is, sir, that you just chose not to. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You're simply saying whatever pleases you, and I'm telling you no. I certainly wasn't a commander who in Afghanistan would have taken so many people away in order to pound the Taliban. Here you have to compare the armies and not come up with any sort of organisation for the HVO as you saw fit. There are parallel systems, various users, what a commander should do in a given area, be they American, French, or Croatian -- no, no, and no. You can say whatever you like, and I'm telling you no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I allowed the journalists in because I -- I didn't have the right to do that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If you would move to P10924.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is an article from Reuters, Deutscheland, an article that was published on the 7th of September, 1993. He's talking about -- according to UN information, all three war parties have set up detention camps in Bosnia. This according to a report submitted on Tuesday by Tadeusz Mazowiecki, the special reporter of the UN Human Rights Commission. It says in the next paragraph: "According to the Mazowiecki report, in the town of Gabela, south of Capljina, men were locked up in aircraft hangers. Sixteen prisoners survived on daily rations of a cup of watery soup, 650 grams of bread. Former detainees reported that during the summer months, they feared they would suffocate as the hangars were almost sealed airtight." And in this trial, General, we've heard and seen a lot of the evidence about the conditions at Dretelj. Now, General, I asked you a little while about your knowledge about what was going on in these camps, and you denied having any knowledge. How is it possible, General, that as commander of the HVO Main Staff you don't know what is going on in Dretelj, Gabela, but Mr. Mazowiecki knows enough about it to put it into a report that's published in early September?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the form of the question, because we are to then presume that this report is true, accurate, and complete. As I recall, the gentleman never came forward to testify. As I recall, he was never on the Prosecution list. As I recall, he was never offered the opportunity or was subpoenaed to come and refused to come. And therefore to now suggest that everything in this report, albeit comes from a very esteemed individual and is through a highly-esteemed organisation that we are to accept it. It is nothing other than pure hearsay. And so therefore if the gentleman wishes to rephrase the question, I have no problem. But as the question is phrased he's asking the -- first of all, the witness and, indeed, the Trial Chamber to accept what is in the report as fact, as established fact, as judicial facts to be accepted. And to that, I cannot abide by. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me respond. I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Before, Mr. Stringer, you speak, I would only like to say that Mr. Mazowiecki's reports are of public domain, and they have been distributed and used and acknowledged as official documents of the United Nations and of the Security Council, and therefore they have standing. Now, of course I do recognise that here in this case the Prosecution spoke about an article reporting about Mazowiecki's report itself, so from this point of view, it is true that it has a certain -- certain standing which is not only so official as the documents what I mentioned. But anyway, those issues which were raised by Mr. Mazowiecki are -- have been well-known within the UN, within the General Assembly of the UN, and of the Security Council itself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I accept the comments of Judge Prandler. My point is slightly different. It is not whether the gentleman said it. We all know that the UN said a lot of things and it came out especially during the scandal with oil for -- for food, that a lot of folks working for the UN were simply lying and stealing. We know that. And to suggest that every UN document has a certain cachet value that we are to accept and not challenge in a court of law, I think that would be the wrong approach. Now, I fully understand Mr. Stringer's right to say in this report he's making these representations. Now, assuming these are correct, then he can go on. But to say since they are in the report and because it's to the UN by the UN for the UN, we must therefore say that these are true, accurate, and complete facts, I think in a court of law that should not be the case. Facts have to be proved. People make mistakes, but I do take your point, Your Honour, and I do think that Mr. Stringer is perfectly capable of using the material if he slightly reformulates his question. We're seeing a superb advocate quickly thinking on his feet and even entertaining us sometimes with some sound-bytes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, it should be clear, and I don't have the question on my screen any more. I mean, this goes to the knowledge of the general, notice, information that's out there that would be available that would put the general or anyone else on notice of the events, the situation that's being reported in the press by Mazowiecki. Now, clearly the Trial Chamber will ultimately have to conclude whether the conditions -- whether the information that's reflected in the report or whether the conditions as asserted by the Prosecution have been moved, but the point is, and I asked the general this, how is it possible that he doesn't know when it's in the press and when Mazowiecki knows or is reporting it? So, you know, I guess I concede counsel's point that ultimately it's for the Trial Chamber to decide, but with respect, I don't think I asked the question that way. The question is about notice. And I would assert, Mr. President, it's a fair question to ask the general how is it that he doesn't know when these are in the reports in the media, these are things being written by others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please ask him the question. And I would like to remind everyone that this debate already took place on several months or perhaps several weeks ago. It was said by the Defence, and I remember this very clearly, that reports from the UN can only be valid according to what had been purported to be said to the reporter or to the drafter of the report. So this has already been said. But the question that is raised is to know whether Mr. Praljak knew about the report, about press reports and so on and so forth. So we are in this area. Please proceed, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, let me put -- let me put it to you again. The fact is the information was out there. It was readily available to anyone in the media, and it was readily available to you. You were on notice. You knew about these things, didn't you General? Or at the very least you knew enough to put you on notice that you needed to look into it and deal with it yourself. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please try to break this down? Was I supposed to be careful? Was I supposed to look into it? At what time exactly? Let's take this one step at a time and then I can answer. This way, I don't think so. One by one, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, you had notice that there were situations involving prisoners at all of these facilities that you as the commander of the HVO were obligated to look into. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean there were situations? What do you mean by there were situations? Can you please explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I'm not going to fence with you on this. Let's move to the next part of this document. It says in the next paragraph --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reads here General Slobodan Praljak stated his soldiers were holding no prisoners at all. This document that I'm being shown. General Slobodan Praljak stated that his soldiers were holding no prisoners at all. That's probably what I said at the time to this person. The soldiers under my command were holding no prisoners at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, the fact is that the HVO were holding hundreds if not -- well, hundreds of prisoners still in the Heliodrom, Gabela, Ljubuski; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by what I said. The soldiers under my command were holding no prisoners at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Well, here you say that your soldiers were no longer holding any prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may intervene. Prisoners of war, POW. Now, Mr. Stringer, are you suggesting that the prisoners held in Gabela and Dretelj were all POWs? Or is it possible, Mr. Praljak, that they were other prisoners but not POWs technically? Could you have meant that when you said that you held no POW?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know, sir. I can't answer that one. It's not that we were no longer holding any prisoners at all. It reads: "They were holding no prisoners at all." The HVO soldiers under my command. That's crystal clear. Anything else --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm ready to move to the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, we have a press release from Reuters, which is a news agency of high repute. Their correspondent based in Sarajevo reports on the 7th of September in Sarajevo, and he quotes the Mazowiecki report, and then you seem to appear in the report as well. If this journalist has done his duty, you should have had some contact with the Reuters journalist, and he must have asked you some questions saying, Well, there is a UN report talking about this and that. Do you remember having being interviewed precisely on those points because here some words are put into your mouth. But when a journalist is doing his work properly, there are some commas, inverted commas to show that it is a quote. So there is no certainty that you responded. We are asking you what may have happened 15 years ago, and I realise that this might not be realistic, but do you remember a journalist calling you or interviewing you on this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember. I can't remember, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have another question then. I believe I asked the same question to other witnesses. All we have to do is look at the transcripts. We have this report which has been covered by the press, and we realised that there are prisoners on all sides, and there are 1.220 Serbs [as interpreted] that are detained by the BiH in 24 camps. So we have Croats that are detained. Information of this nature should have been brought to the attention of the authorities, whether it was in Zagreb or elsewhere. And my assumption is that it had been brought to the attention of the Zagreb authorities who learned about that. At this stage or at that stage, rather, did someone call to say there is a problem in Zagreb? Do you remember, or do you not remember.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction from the interpreter it was 1.220 Croats.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't. I remember that one missing sentence about the partial nature. If you lose site of the fact that the Muslim offensive continued even more fiercely on the 15th and the 16th of September, perhaps one might say you could have done this or you could have done that. But then for the next 25 or 30 days around Vrde and all that, I hardly left the front line throughout that time. The only way you can get at the truth is if you look at the whole. If you take a partial view of one thing at a time, it can mislead you. I never had lunch with Petkovic. I never slept in the same bed for two consecutive nights. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit is P05104, 15 September 1993. President Boban issues an order. The order is directed towards the Defence Department and the Main Staff of the armed forces of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Now, in item 3 he orders: "In the prisoners of war detention centres where the conditions required by the international war law and Geneva Convention are not ensured, they should immediately be introduced, and prisoners of war must be treated in accordance with the provisions of the Geneva Convention and other humanitarian standards." He orders the ICRC is to be allowed free visits to detention centres for prisoners of war, flow of humanitarian aid. Item number 7 he orders: "The HVO Main Staff will inform all subordinated commands and units of this order and provide professional help in its implementation." Now, just to continue on with this, General, and then we'll talk about it all, the next exhibit is P05188, which if you would look at that one I'd suggest then is you issuing this order as you've been directed by Mr. Boban, sending his order down to all operative zones, all units subordinated to the Main Staff, and to the chief of the military police. All right. Do you remember this, General? Do you remember receiving this order from Mr. Boban and then sending it down the chain of command as is indicated here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to the first question, did I receive Mr. Boban's order, this one, the answer is yes. Did I forward it down the chain of command, no. I left out items 3, 4, 5 from Boban's order because they had nothing whatsoever to do with the Main Staff. I received Mr. Boban's order and I conveyed to the lower levels --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. We're going to talk about that. Let me ask you some questions first about the Boban order. You do recall receiving this on or about September 15th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, we just looked at the Reuters article from September 7th, which is a week prior, in which you say that your soldiers are no longer holding any prisoners of war. So, General, do you know what prisoners of war Mr. Boban --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say "no longer." It doesn't say "no longer." It says "not at all." You keep saying no longer. It's like they were holding prisoners of war and now they are no longer holding prisoners of war, whereas it reads they were not holding any prisoners of war at --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Can the interpreters please be allowed the time to finish interpreting General Praljak. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we a moment's break, please, until you clear this up.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because in the English and the German, it reads exactly the way Mr. Stringer is saying, but it was translated into Croatian as there were no prisoners there without the "no longer" bit. So the General is working with one text and Mr. Stringer is working with a different text. That's why the discrepancy has arisen and the excitement, too, on the part of Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In German "mehr fest" does not mean any longer. "Seine Soldaten heilten keine Kriegsgefangenen mehr fest," but that is not correct, because it should read "are not holding" instead of "are no longer holding."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, where is the German text? I don't have the German text, and I --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The German text --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: There is a chance I would understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It should be there. It's the original language of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The very end. The last document is in German. In P --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Judge Antonetti, a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I inform everyone that the Registrar was telling us we still have 20 minutes worth of tape. So we will have to stop at five to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether and to what extent, if so, I have to take an oath and take an expert or interpreter's stand. I have the German text in front of me, and maybe I'll read it in German and then under the control of all other linguists here give a translation. The German text reads: "Der Kommandeur der bosnischen Kroaten, General Slobodan Praljak, erkldrte hingegen, seine Soldaten hielten keine Kriegsgefangenen mehr fest," which translated to the extent that it is important would say: "Did not hold any prisoners of war any more," which is -- and the meaning is the same as "do no longer hold." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour, and that's where the problem lay, because the general in the Croatian interpretation didn't have this "mehr," "more," or "longer." So Mr. Stringer was adhering to where it says "longer" or "more," and in the Croatian there was no -- this word was not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, looking at P05104, which is the order from Mate Boban to the Main Staff and the Defence Department, I think my last question to you was whether you recall receiving this document on or about the 15th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, in item number 3, he says: "The prisoners of war --" well, I won't read it again. I read it before we had the interruption. But what's saying is that they have to ensure that the applicable -- required conditions applicable to prisoners of war must be ensured --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not receiving an interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll start again. In paragraph 3, what Boban's saying there is that wherever the conditions are not in accordance with law for the prisoners of war, those conditions have to be fixed centrally. Now, General, you saw this, so doesn't this tell you that there are prisoners of war, HVO prisoners of war, who were being held in places where the conditions may not be in accordance with international law?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says in which possibly not all conditions have been ensured and so on. Yes, I did of course read this, and I gave you an answer to that question and you can see that from my order. Now, you want to introduce a totalitarian society, and I had nothing to do with items 3, 4, and 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So the answer here is despite the information contained in this document or the suggestion that all is not well with prisoners of war, you did nothing with that information because you considered that it was someone else's job, not yours; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I read this information. Now, what the situation was, what should be improved, and what was actually happened, I did not have any information, and I had nothing to do with this in the post that I held, structural, under law, or prescribed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And as you've already indicated, we see that when you sent Boban's order down your chain of command, down as he directed, this is P05188, you in fact made no reference at all to the treatment of prisoners; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I refer to prisoners and conduct towards prisoners when the soldiers that I commanded did -- had nothing to do with any kinds of prisoners? So why would I write something in my order --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- like that that was incomprehensible?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So since the Defence Department is the other recipient of this order from Boban, are you telling us, General, then that it was the Defence Department that was responsible for the implementation of this order in respect of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm saying exactly this: The Main Staff was not responsible, and I don't want to speak about matters here in court about which I'm not fully certain. Therefore, I don't know. My answer is I do not know precisely and fully the kind of responsibility over these, whatever they were called, prisons of one kind or another, general military or anything similar. I don't know. And I've said that for the umpteenth time, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, the fact is, General, within your own spheres of responsibility and authority, the fact is that both you as the commander of the Main Staff and Mr. Stojic as head of the Defence Department, and Mr. Coric as head of the military police administration, each of you held responsibilities and obligations in respect of prisoners. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely incorrect, and that's precisely what I've been telling you. You want to introduce a totalitarian system, which never existed. A normal society has precisely defined rights and responsibilities for individual matters, and we at least tried to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in a normal society, let me suggest to you that the commander of the armed forces knows who's responsible for prisoners.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true, not even in the American army. The commander does not know what happened in prisons in Iraq. It was the people who did that who were responsible, and he learned about this five months --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: You don't have to speak now about Iraq and about the American army. You have to speak about yourself and what you have done. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I'm asking you about who knows what they're responsible for. You say you're not responsible for prisoners. You claim that you don't know who is, and I'm putting to you that that's absurd, and that in any political-military organisation everyone knows, certainly at your level, who's responsible for what. And if you claim you're not responsible for prisoners, the fact is you know who is and you just refuse to say it, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. I don't have to know who was responsible for prisoners. And, please, Judge Prandler, there are regulations and rules in armies, and you can't set this one apart. You have to know how each army operates in order to hold people accountable. If you want to set up a separate system for this army, you can do what you like. But I claim that it is not true either for the American army or the others. Those who committed crimes in Abu Ghraib, it wasn't the commander of the army who was held responsible but the perpetrators of those crimes because he wasn't informed about what was going on and it was journalists who uncovered it. And here it's my right to defend myself by using logics and general knowledge, general well knowledge, but not only for the HVO but something that holds true for everyone and all armies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I have a follow-up question. As an impartial trier of fact I must examine both versions, the case presented by the Prosecution and the case presented by the Defence. This is how an impartial Judge does his work. And in order to do this, I examine the Prosecutor's case. He is showing us two documents, an order from Mr. Boban and your own order. And the Prosecutor notes that paragraphs 3, 4, and 5 are missing in your own document. Because of this anyone seeing both documents could very well - and here I say could only - could very well draw the conclusions that General Praljak completely set aside this part regarding prisoners. Actually, turned a blind eye on it. And he did this deliberately. That is one interpretation of the documents. Second interpretation. You became aware of Mate Boban's order. You gave instructions to the person drafting the order. I'm sure you're not the person who actually took a quill to write all this, and the person drafting the order is executing orders given by you, and you can give him the order not to copy paragraphs 3, 4, and 5. And you might have told the person drafting the document, "Because this is not of my responsibility." That is one assumption that would back what you're saying. You might believe that it is somebody else's business and that you have nothing to relay regarding points 3, 4, and 5. Now, as -- in your recollection, can you tell us whether you asked the person drafting the document for you to set aside items 3, 4, and 5, or is it that person who actually drafted the whole document and just signed it blindly? Do you remember anything about the way you drafted this order? There are two ways of looking at this, obviously. One is in incriminatory, the other one exculpatory, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it is pot possible. An order by the president of the HZ-HB and the supreme commander of the armed forces is read. I didn't write this, but it was read pursuant [indiscernible] orders, leave out items that have nothing to do with the responsibilities and rights of the Main Staff of the HVO. Your Honours, responsibility begins with appointments and dismissals, and you send the responsible person the reports. How can you be responsible if you don't have the right to replace, dismiss, incarcerate, and so on? You can't. And if you're not receiving any reports, it means you're not in the reporting structure. That's true for courts. That's true for everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you are not answering my question. It was a very specific question. I wanted to know whether you gave orders to the person drafting the document, orders by which paragraphs 3, 4, 5 of Mr. Boban -- on prisoners to be excluded for -- on grounds that you were not competent for this matter, or whether this other person actually drafted the entire document by himself and you thought it was fine. What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I gave you an answer precisely. I don't know whether it was recorded and translated. I ordered that he throw out items that have nothing to do with the commander and the Main Staff of the HVO. That's what I said. I don't know why there was no interpretation, but I did answer that in very precise terms and quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry that I have to say I read these two documents in a different way than the President. In your order you say in the first introductory paragraph that you have enclosed the order of Mate Boban. There is no reference to any redaction of that order, and I must suppose that you enclosed the order of Mate Boban the way you had received it. Is that a correct assumption?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, sir. Mate Boban is sending his order to two addressees, and I attach his order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. The question is much simpler. You write an order signed "Praljak." You do not deny that you signed this. You say in this order that the order of Mate Boban is enclosed. So am I right in assuming that the recipient of your order gets your order and attached to it a copy of the order of Mate Boban as it was, original copied without changes? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. Correct, yes, a copy of Mate Boban's order and my order over the units that I command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Then in number 3 of your order you comment on numbers 5 and 6 of the order of Mate Boban; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. I say that they must be as they stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I did not see in your order any reference at all to other numbers in Mate Boban's order. You do not comment specifically on any of the other points.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Right. So that -- it follows that when you told us that you did not hand on the order, carry on -- carry further to your subordinates the order to the extent that it concerns prisoners, this is your interpretation of your order, but there is no tangible trace of this. It's just, you say -- I suppose, I'm putting it to you, you say, As this was not my business, automatically those who received from me Boban's orders also would disregard it because it did not concern the army, full stop. Is that I way I should understand your argument?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. I with like to put on the transcript that I do not share the content of this question. I don't agree with it, because it's too complex, and I believe that we should continue -- resume with all this tomorrow. This is extremely complicated, and we're almost at the end of the tape. We will have to take a look at the transcript, but we have no tape left, or hardly any. So we will meet again tomorrow morning at 9.00 a.m. in this courtroom. Thank you.
